questions.stem: Which age term does Guideline 5 use for neonates, following the American Academy of Pediatrics?
options: Postmenstrual age = gestational age + chronological age
Corrected age = chronological age minus 40 weeks
Conceptional age = gestational age + chronological age
questions.explanation: Record gestational, chronological and postmenstrual age in weeks. Postmenstrual age is gestational age plus chronological age; the AAP advises against the term conceptional age.
questions.memoryAid: POST-MENSTRUAL = GA + CA. 'Conceptional' is OUT.
questions.author: NeuroLinea Focus Drills (AI-drafted, fact-checked; requires expert review)

questions.stem: What sensitivity does Guideline 6 require when recording for electrocerebral inactivity?
options: 2 µV peak to peak for 10 min
questions.explanation: Record at 2 µV/mm or more sensitive (for example 1 µV/mm) for at least 30 min, with a calibration of 2 or 5 µV. Note the unit: 2 µV/mm is the sensitivity; 2 µV peak to peak is the voltage threshold for ECI.
questions.memoryAid: ECI = TWO and THIRTY: 2 µV/mm for 30 minutes.
questions.author: NeuroLinea Focus Drills (AI-drafted, fact-checked; requires expert review)

questions.stem: What interelectrode distance does Guideline 6 require for ECI montages?
options: At most 5 cm, using closely spaced pairs
At least 10 cm, using double-distance pairs such as Fp1-C3
Any distance, as long as all channels are referential
questions.explanation: Longer distances record more of a low-voltage field, so ECI montages use pairs at least 10 cm apart (double-distance links such as Fp1-C3 and C3-O1). A full electrode set including Fz, Cz and Pz is needed; a 1- or 2-channel device is not acceptable.
questions.memoryAid: TEN cm APART to hear a whisper.
questions.author: NeuroLinea Focus Drills (AI-drafted, fact-checked; requires expert review)

questions.stem: How is the integrity of the whole recording system tested during an ECI study?
options: Touching each electrode to make an artifact
Raising the high-frequency filter to 100 Hz
Checking every impedance once at the start
questions.explanation: Touching each electrode in turn proves that every channel is connected and displaying. Impedances must be between 100 and 10,000 Ω; machine noise is checked with a 10,000 Ω resistor across the inputs, and an ECG and noncephalic (dorsum of the hand) monitor are added.
questions.memoryAid: TOUCH TEST: tap each lead, see it jump, then you know it is live.
questions.author: NeuroLinea Focus Drills (AI-drafted, fact-checked; requires expert review)

questions.stem: Which filter settings does Guideline 6 allow during an ECI recording?
options: LFF 5 Hz to remove sweat; HFF 70 Hz
HFF no lower than 30 Hz; LFF no higher than 1 Hz
Notch on throughout; HFF and LFF unchanged
HFF 15 Hz to remove muscle; LFF 1 Hz
questions.explanation: HFF no lower than 30 Hz and LFF no higher than 1 Hz. If the notch filter is used, part of the record must also be made without it. Intense somatosensory, auditory and visual stimuli are applied and annotated.
questions.memoryAid: ECI filters: THIRTY up, ONE down, and show it once WITHOUT the notch.
questions.author: NeuroLinea Focus Drills (AI-drafted, fact-checked; requires expert review)

questions.stem: If ECI is in doubt, when should the study be repeated?
options: 6 h later in adults, 24 h in children
24 h later in adults, 6 h in children
Never; a single study is always final
questions.explanation: Guideline 6: repeat after at least 6 h in adults and at least 24 h in neonates and children. Also document temperature, blood pressure, oxygen saturation, all medications, the last sedative dose and toxicology, because drugs and hypothermia can mimic ECI.
questions.memoryAid: SIX hours for grown-ups, a whole DAY for the young.
questions.author: NeuroLinea Focus Drills (AI-drafted, fact-checked; requires expert review)

questions.stem: In which section of a Guideline 7 report does premedication and its dose belong?
questions.explanation: The five sections are History, Technical Description, EEG Description, Impression and Clinical Correlation. The technical description covers date and place, number of electrodes, 10-20 or 10-10 placement, extra or moved electrodes, premedication with dose, sleep deprivation and state.
questions.memoryAid: Five parts, H-T-E-I-C: 'Have The EEG Interpreted Clearly'.
questions.author: NeuroLinea Focus Drills (AI-drafted, fact-checked; requires expert review)

questions.stem: How does Guideline 7 structure the Impression?
options: A full description of the background, then the artifacts
Normal or abnormal first, then the main abnormalities ranked
The technologist's opinion, then the physician's
questions.explanation: The impression states normal or abnormal first, then ranks the main abnormalities (preferably no more than three or four). The clinical correlation explains the meaning in plain language and gives no specific treatment orders.
questions.memoryAid: IMPRESSION: verdict FIRST, then the TOP three.
questions.author: NeuroLinea Focus Drills (AI-drafted, fact-checked; requires expert review)

questions.stem: According to Guideline 7, when should artifacts be mentioned in the report?
options: Only when caused by equipment failure
When they mimic, swamp, block or help the reading
Every artifact, each listed with its time
Not at all, since artifacts are not cerebral
questions.explanation: Artifacts are reported when they mimic cerebral activity, are excessive, interfere (more than 50% of the tracing in more than 50% of electrodes) or are diagnostically useful.
questions.memoryAid: Report the artifact that FOOLS, FLOODS, BLOCKS or HELPS.
questions.author: NeuroLinea Focus Drills (AI-drafted, fact-checked; requires expert review)

questions.stem: The 2021 ACNS Critical Care EEG Terminology applies to which patients?
questions.explanation: The 2021 terminology (Hirsch et al.) replaced the 2012 version and is used for all ages except neonates, who have a separate ACNS terminology. It added ESz, ESE, ECSz, ECSE, BIRDs, IIC, UI, identical bursts, CAPE and extreme delta brush.
questions.memoryAid: 2021 is for EVERYONE but the NEWBORN.
questions.author: NeuroLinea Focus Drills (AI-drafted, fact-checked; requires expert review)

questions.stem: Rhythmic delta is bilaterally synchronous and symmetric but limited to both frontal regions. What is Main Term 1?
questions.explanation: Generalized means any bilaterally synchronous and symmetric pattern, even with a restricted field such as bifrontal. A region at least 50% higher in voltage earns a predominance label: frontally, occipitally or midline predominant.
questions.memoryAid: SYNC + SYMMETRIC = G, even if it only covers the FRONT.
questions.author: NeuroLinea Focus Drills (AI-drafted, fact-checked; requires expert review)

questions.stem: A bilateral pattern is synchronous but clearly and consistently higher on the right. How is it classed?
questions.explanation: Generalized must also be symmetric. A bilateral pattern clearly and consistently larger on one side (bilateral asymmetric), or with a consistent lead-in from the same side (bilateral asynchronous), is lateralized. Shifting predominance that is not consistently (over 80%) on one side stays generalized.
questions.memoryAid: LOPSIDED is LATERALIZED, even when both sides fire.
questions.author: NeuroLinea Focus Drills (AI-drafted, fact-checked; requires expert review)

questions.stem: Two independent periodic patterns occur at the same time in the same hemisphere. Which Main Term 1 is used?
questions.explanation: UI, new in 2021, is two independent patterns in the same hemisphere at the same time. BI is one in each hemisphere at the same time. Mf needs at least three independent lateralized patterns with at least one in each hemisphere.
questions.memoryAid: U = Unilateral = ONE side, TWO patterns. B = Both sides. Mf = Many (3+).
questions.author: NeuroLinea Focus Drills (AI-drafted, fact-checked; requires expert review)

questions.stem: How many independent lateralized patterns are needed for 'multifocal'?
options: Three or more, with each hemisphere involved
Two or more, both in the same hemisphere
Two, with one in each hemisphere
questions.explanation: Multifocal is at least three independent lateralized patterns, at least one in each hemisphere, all occurring at the same time. Independent patterns at different times (left one hour, right later) are two lateralized patterns, not BI or Mf.
questions.memoryAid: MULTI = THREE or more, and BOTH sides represented.
questions.author: NeuroLinea Focus Drills (AI-drafted, fact-checked; requires expert review)

questions.stem: Sharp waves each followed by a slow wave repeat with a clear, flat interval between complexes. Which Main Term 2 fits?
questions.explanation: SW requires the slow wave to be followed immediately by the next complex, with no interval. Once there is a clear interval between discharges recurring at nearly regular intervals, the pattern is PDs.
questions.memoryAid: A GAP makes it PERIODIC. No gap = SW.
questions.author: NeuroLinea Focus Drills (AI-drafted, fact-checked; requires expert review)

questions.stem: What is the minimum duration for a pattern to qualify as rhythmic or periodic?
questions.explanation: At least 6 consecutive cycles (for example 1 Hz for 6 s, or 3 Hz for 2 s). Three cycles is the minimum for each step of evolution, a common source of confusion.
questions.memoryAid: SIX to COUNT, THREE to STEP.
questions.author: NeuroLinea Focus Drills (AI-drafted, fact-checked; requires expert review)

questions.stem: How does the 2021 terminology define 'nearly regular' (rhythmic or periodic)?
options: Each discharge has the same number of phases
Period varies under 10% across the pattern
Every cycle is exactly the same length
Period varies under 50% in most cycle pairs
questions.explanation: Rhythmic or periodic means the period varies by less than 50% from one cycle to the next in most (over 50%) cycle pairs. It does not require identical cycles, a fixed number of phases or a fixed duration.
questions.memoryAid: Under HALF a change, in more than HALF the pairs.
questions.author: NeuroLinea Focus Drills (AI-drafted, fact-checked; requires expert review)

questions.stem: Rhythmic, regular 1.5 Hz delta is seen over the left hemisphere only. What is it named?
questions.explanation: Lateralized (L) + rhythmic delta activity (RDA) = LRDA. RDA must have a fairly uniform shape and duration with no interval between waves, at 0.5 to 4 Hz; irregular or polymorphic delta is not RDA.
questions.memoryAid: Build the NAME like LEGO: where (L) + what (RDA).
questions.author: NeuroLinea Focus Drills (AI-drafted, fact-checked; requires expert review)

questions.stem: A pattern is present in 30% of a recording epoch. What is its prevalence?
questions.explanation: Prevalence: continuous at least 90%; abundant 50 to 89%; frequent 10 to 49%; occasional 1 to 9%; rare under 1%.
questions.memoryAid: Prevalence 1-10-50-90: rare, occasional, FREQUENT, abundant, continuous.
questions.author: NeuroLinea Focus Drills (AI-drafted, fact-checked; requires expert review)

questions.stem: A run of a pattern lasts 5 minutes. Which duration category applies?
questions.explanation: Duration: very long at least 1 h; long 10 to 59 min; intermediate 1 to 9.9 min; brief 10 to 59 s; very brief under 10 s.
questions.memoryAid: Seconds BRIEF, minutes MIDDLE, tens of minutes LONG, an hour VERY long.
questions.author: NeuroLinea Focus Drills (AI-drafted, fact-checked; requires expert review)

questions.stem: A periodic discharge has a duration of 120 ms measured at the baseline. How is its sharpness classed?
questions.explanation: Sharpness applies to PDs and SW only and is measured at the baseline: spiky under 70 ms, sharp 70 to 200 ms, sharply contoured (sharp shape but too long), blunt (smooth or sinusoidal).
questions.memoryAid: Same cut-offs as spikes and sharp waves: 70 and 200 ms.
questions.author: NeuroLinea Focus Drills (AI-drafted, fact-checked; requires expert review)

questions.stem: A pattern's discharges measure 90 µV peak to trough on longitudinal bipolar. Which absolute amplitude category applies?
questions.explanation: Absolute amplitude: very low under 20 µV, low 20 to 49 µV, medium 50 to 149 µV, high at least 150 µV, measured peak to trough in longitudinal bipolar. Relative amplitude (PDs only) compares the discharge with the background between discharges: 2 or less, or more than 2.
questions.memoryAid: 20-50-150: very low, low, MEDIUM, high.
questions.author: NeuroLinea Focus Drills (AI-drafted, fact-checked; requires expert review)

questions.stem: Which change counts as evolution under the 2021 terminology?
options: A steady rise in amplitude over 2 minutes
A single 1 Hz change in frequency
Two 0.5 Hz steps one way, 3+ cycles each
Three back-and-forth changes in a minute
questions.explanation: Evolution needs at least two unequivocal sequential changes in one category (frequency, morphology or location), each step lasting at least 3 cycles, without the feature staying unchanged for 5 min or more. Amplitude change alone is not evolution. Back-and-forth changes are fluctuation.
questions.memoryAid: EVOLVING goes ONE WAY, TWO steps, 3 cycles each. Bigger is not evolving.
questions.author: NeuroLinea Focus Drills (AI-drafted, fact-checked; requires expert review)

questions.stem: A pattern changes 1 to 1.5 to 1 to 1.5 Hz, each change within a minute of the last. How is it described?
questions.explanation: Fluctuating means three or more changes no more than 1 min apart in frequency (at least 0.5 Hz), morphology or location (at least one interelectrode distance), without meeting the criteria for evolution. Static is neither evolving nor fluctuating.
questions.memoryAid: FLUCTUATING goes UP and DOWN like a yo-yo; EVOLVING marches ONE way.
questions.author: NeuroLinea Focus Drills (AI-drafted, fact-checked; requires expert review)

questions.stem: LPDs appear reproducibly each time the nurse rouses the patient. How is this coded?
questions.explanation: Stimulus-induced (SI-) means reproducibly brought on or made worse by an alerting stimulus; stimulus-terminated (ST-) means reproducibly stopped. SIRPIDs is the umbrella term, but the specific pattern should be named, with the type of stimulus recorded.
questions.memoryAid: SI = Stimulus IN (starts it); ST = Stimulus sTops it.
questions.author: NeuroLinea Focus Drills (AI-drafted, fact-checked; requires expert review)

questions.stem: Which plus modifier can be applied to rhythmic delta activity but not to periodic discharges?
questions.explanation: +F (superimposed fast) applies to PDs or RDA; +R applies to PDs only; +S applies to RDA only; combined forms are +FR for PDs and +FS for RDA. Plus modifiers never apply to SW. A pattern that is both PDs and RDA with similar prominence is coded PDs+R, not RDA+S.
questions.memoryAid: PDs get R, RDA gets S; F fits both; SW gets NOTHING.
questions.author: NeuroLinea Focus Drills (AI-drafted, fact-checked; requires expert review)

questions.stem: Abundant rhythmic delta with fast activity locked to each delta wave is called what?
options: Delta brush of prematurity, a normal variant
Extreme delta brush, a subtype of +F
questions.explanation: Extreme delta brush is a subtype of +F: abundant or continuous RDA+F (or blunt-delta PDs+F) with fast activity locked to the delta wave, classically described in anti-NMDA receptor encephalitis.
questions.memoryAid: EXTREME delta BRUSH = a fast BRISTLE riding EVERY delta wave.
questions.author: NeuroLinea Focus Drills (AI-drafted, fact-checked; requires expert review)

questions.stem: What is the current 2021 name for the pattern once called FIRDA?
questions.explanation: FIRDA became frontally predominant GRDA. Other replacements: PLEDs became LPDs, BIPLEDs became BIPDs, GPEDs became GPDs, semirhythmic delta became quasi-RDA, and 'subclinical' seizure became 'nonconvulsive'. The 'E' for epileptiform was dropped because many periodic patterns are not epileptic.
questions.memoryAid: Old letters OUT: PLEDs → LPDs, FIRDA → frontal GRDA, drop the E.
questions.author: NeuroLinea Focus Drills (AI-drafted, fact-checked; requires expert review)

questions.stem: How does the 2021 terminology handle 'triphasic waves'?
questions.explanation: Triphasic morphology is a minor modifier, not a pattern name: negative-positive-negative, each phase longer than the one before, with the positive phase highest.
questions.memoryAid: TRIPHASIC is a SHAPE, not a NAME: GPDs with triphasic morphology.
questions.author: NeuroLinea Focus Drills (AI-drafted, fact-checked; requires expert review)

questions.stem: Which pattern meets the 2021 definition of an electrographic seizure (ESz)?
options: Rhythmic delta lasting at least 5 s
Discharges over 2.5 Hz for 10 s or more
questions.explanation: ESz: epileptiform discharges averaging more than 2.5 Hz for at least 10 s (more than 25 discharges in 10 s), or any pattern with definite evolution lasting at least 10 s. PDs or SW above 2.5 Hz for 10 s or more are seizures, not PDs.
questions.memoryAid: Seizure 10 / 2.5 / 25: over 2.5 Hz, 10 seconds, 25 discharges.
questions.author: NeuroLinea Focus Drills (AI-drafted, fact-checked; requires expert review)

questions.stem: When does seizure activity become electrographic status epilepticus (ESE)?
options: 10 continuous min, or 20% of any hour
questions.explanation: ESE is ESz for at least 10 continuous minutes, or for a total of at least 20% of any 60-minute period. A frequent mistake is to give 30 minutes.
questions.memoryAid: TEN straight, or a FIFTH of an hour (12 minutes total).
questions.author: NeuroLinea Focus Drills (AI-drafted, fact-checked; requires expert review)

questions.stem: Which statement about an electroclinical seizure (ECSz) is correct?
options: Only when EEG improves and the patient does not
Any length, if a clinical sign is time-locked
Only when the rhythm is faster than 4 Hz
At least 10 s, the same as an ESz
questions.explanation: ECSz is any EEG pattern with a definite time-locked clinical correlate (any duration), or EEG and clinical improvement after a parenteral antiseizure medication. An ECSz can be shorter than 10 s; an ESz cannot. 'Nonconvulsive' is preferred over 'subclinical'.
questions.memoryAid: Clinical sign + EEG = seizure at ANY length. EEG alone needs 10 s.
questions.author: NeuroLinea Focus Drills (AI-drafted, fact-checked; requires expert review)

questions.stem: With bilateral tonic-clonic activity, how long must an electroclinical seizure last to be electroclinical status epilepticus?
questions.explanation: ECSE is ECSz for at least 10 continuous minutes or at least 20% of any 60 minutes, but with bilateral tonic-clonic activity 5 continuous minutes is enough, matching the ILAE 2015 t1 of 5 min for tonic-clonic status (t2 30 min).
questions.memoryAid: CONVULSING? FIVE minutes is status.
questions.author: NeuroLinea Focus Drills (AI-drafted, fact-checked; requires expert review)

questions.stem: Which description fits BIRDs (brief potentially ictal rhythmic discharges)?
options: Over 4 Hz, 0.5 to under 10 s, with evolution, a match or sharp contour
Periodic discharges at 1 Hz lasting more than 10 seconds
Any normal variant that lasts less than 10 seconds
Rhythmic delta under 4 Hz lasting about one minute
questions.explanation: BIRDs: focal or generalized rhythmic activity over 4 Hz (at least 6 waves at a regular rate), lasting 0.5 s to under 10 s, not a normal variant or part of burst suppression, without a definite clinical correlate, and with evolution, a match to the patient's discharges or seizures, or sharp contour. The same evolving rhythm for 10 s or more is a seizure.
questions.memoryAid: BIRDs are FAST and BRIEF: over 4 Hz, under 10 s.
questions.author: NeuroLinea Focus Drills (AI-drafted, fact-checked; requires expert review)

questions.stem: BIRDs that are sharply contoured but neither evolve nor match the patient's seizures are classed as what?
questions.explanation: Definite BIRDs show evolution, or the same morphology and location as the patient's interictal discharges or seizures. Sharply contoured BIRDs without either are possible BIRDs.
questions.memoryAid: EVOLVES or MATCHES = DEFINITE; only SHARP = POSSIBLE.
questions.author: NeuroLinea Focus Drills (AI-drafted, fact-checked; requires expert review)

questions.stem: Which pattern meets criterion A of the ictal-interictal continuum (IIC)?
options: Periodic discharges averaging more than 1.0 and up to 2.5 Hz over 10 seconds
GRDA at 1.5 Hz with no plus modifier
Periodic discharges averaging more than 2.5 Hz for 10 seconds
questions.explanation: IIC criterion A: any PD or SW pattern averaging more than 1.0 and up to 2.5 Hz over 10 s (more than 10 and up to 25 discharges in 10 s). Criterion B is 0.5 to 1 Hz with a plus modifier or fluctuation. Above 2.5 Hz for 10 s it is already a seizure, and IIC excludes anything meeting ESz or ESE.
questions.memoryAid: IIC sits BETWEEN 1 and 2.5 Hz: below a seizure, above plain PDs.
questions.author: NeuroLinea Focus Drills (AI-drafted, fact-checked; requires expert review)

questions.stem: Under IIC criterion C, which rhythmic delta pattern is excluded?
questions.explanation: Criterion C covers lateralized RDA (LRDA, BIRDA, UIRDA, MfRDA) averaging more than 1 Hz for at least 10 s with a plus modifier or fluctuation. GRDA is not included. IIC is a purely electrographic term (possible ESz or ESE), not a diagnosis.
questions.memoryAid: IIC rhythmic delta must be ONE-SIDED: GRDA does not count.
questions.author: NeuroLinea Focus Drills (AI-drafted, fact-checked; requires expert review)

questions.stem: The left hemisphere is consistently 60% lower in voltage than the right on a referential montage. How is the symmetry classed?
options: It cannot be classed without a bipolar montage
questions.explanation: Marked asymmetry is a voltage difference of 50% or more, or a frequency difference of more than 1 Hz. Mild is under 50% or 0.5 to 1 Hz. Voltage asymmetry is judged on an appropriate referential recording, because bipolar subtraction can hide or create asymmetry.
questions.memoryAid: HALF or more = MARKED; check it REFERENTIALLY.
questions.author: NeuroLinea Focus Drills (AI-drafted, fact-checked; requires expert review)

questions.stem: Which rule applies to the posterior dominant rhythm in the 2021 terminology?
options: It counts whether or not it blocks with eye opening
It is measured in the first half-second after eye closure
It must block with eye opening; measured over 1 s after closure
It is reported to the nearest 2 Hz, without reactivity
questions.explanation: The PDR must attenuate with eye opening to qualify. Measure it more than 1 s after eye closure to avoid alpha squeak, and report it to the nearest 0.5 Hz as present, absent or unclear.
questions.memoryAid: WAIT ONE SECOND after closing: squeak first, true rhythm after.
questions.author: NeuroLinea Focus Drills (AI-drafted, fact-checked; requires expert review)

questions.stem: Bursts of 2 s alternate with 8 s of suppression. How is continuity classed?
questions.explanation: Continuity by percentage of the record attenuated or suppressed: continuous under 1%, nearly continuous 1 to 9%, discontinuous 10 to 49%, burst attenuation or suppression 50 to 99%, attenuation or suppression over 99%. Here 8 of every 10 s (80%) is suppressed.
questions.memoryAid: Continuity 1-10-50-99.
questions.author: NeuroLinea Focus Drills (AI-drafted, fact-checked; requires expert review)

questions.stem: What is the difference between 'suppression' and 'attenuation' in the 2021 terminology?
options: Suppression < 20 µV; attenuation < 50 µV whatever the background
They are synonyms used for the same low-voltage periods
Suppression lasts longer; voltage does not separate the two
Suppression < 10 µV; attenuation ≥ 10 µV but < 50% of background
questions.explanation: Suppression: lower-voltage periods under 10 µV. Attenuation: lower-voltage periods of at least 10 µV but under 50% of the higher-voltage background. For overall voltage, suppressed means all activity under 10 µV and low means most activity under 20 µV.
questions.memoryAid: UNDER 10 = SUPPRESSED. Above 10 but under half = ATTENUATED.
questions.author: NeuroLinea Focus Drills (AI-drafted, fact-checked; requires expert review)

questions.stem: What makes a waveform a 'burst' rather than a 'discharge'?
options: It lasts at least 2 s regardless of phases
It lasts at least 0.5 s and has at least 4 phases
questions.explanation: A burst averages at least 0.5 s and has at least 4 phases (at least 3 baseline crossings); shorter or with fewer phases it is a discharge. Bursts can last up to 30 s, and burst and interburst durations are reported.
questions.memoryAid: BURST = half a second and FOUR phases.
questions.author: NeuroLinea Focus Drills (AI-drafted, fact-checked; requires expert review)

questions.stem: When are bursts called 'identical' in the 2021 terminology?
options: First 0.5 s matches in all channels in over 90% of bursts
At least two bursts in the record contain spikes
Every burst has the same peak amplitude throughout
questions.explanation: Identical bursts (new in 2021): the first 0.5 s or more of each burst, or of each stereotyped cluster, looks similar in all channels in over 90% of bursts. Highly epileptiform bursts have 2 or more spikes or sharp waves in most bursts at 1 Hz or faster, or a rhythmic ictal-appearing pattern.
questions.memoryAid: IDENTICAL = the same OPENING half-second, 9 times in 10.
questions.author: NeuroLinea Focus Drills (AI-drafted, fact-checked; requires expert review)

questions.stem: During reactivity testing, only eye-blink and muscle artifact appear after a sternal rub. How is this recorded?
options: SIRPIDs-only, because a stimulus was given
Reactive if the artifact lasts over 1 s
Unreactive: artifact alone does not count
questions.explanation: Reactivity is a change in cerebral EEG activity (voltage or frequency, including attenuation) after stimulation. Muscle or eye-blink artifact alone does not count. Use escalating visual, auditory, tactile and noxious stimuli, annotate each, repeat a second round of noxious stimuli if unreactive, and record sedatives and paralytics.
questions.memoryAid: REACTIVITY lives in the BRAIN waves, not in the BLINKS.
questions.author: NeuroLinea Focus Drills (AI-drafted, fact-checked; requires expert review)

questions.stem: Two background patterns, each at least 10 s long, alternate regularly for at least 6 cycles. What is this called?
questions.explanation: CAPE: two background patterns, each at least 10 s, alternating regularly for at least 6 cycles. State changes (which replaced 'variability') need at least 2 sustained background types related to alertness or stimulation, each lasting at least 60 s.
questions.memoryAid: CAPE = a 10-second SWING, six times over.
questions.author: NeuroLinea Focus Drills (AI-drafted, fact-checked; requires expert review)

questions.stem: Sporadic epileptiform discharges occur about twice a minute. What is their prevalence category?
options: Frequent (at least 1 per minute but under 1 per 10 s)
Occasional (at least 1 per hour but under 1 per minute)
questions.explanation: Sporadic discharges: abundant at least 1 per 10 s (not periodic); frequent at least 1 per minute but under 1 per 10 s; occasional at least 1 per hour but under 1 per minute; rare under 1 per hour.
questions.memoryAid: Per 10 s ABUNDANT, per minute FREQUENT, per hour OCCASIONAL.
questions.author: NeuroLinea Focus Drills (AI-drafted, fact-checked; requires expert review)

questions.stem: How often should the technologist check recording quality during continuous ICU EEG (2015 consensus)?
questions.explanation: Stay at the bedside for the first 20 min and test reactivity, then check recording quality at least twice daily, impedance and scalp daily, and re-gel as needed. Physicians review the first 30 to 60 min as soon as possible, then at least twice daily, with a written report at least every 24 h.
questions.memoryAid: cEEG: 20 minutes at the bed, TWICE a day the check, a report EVERY day.
questions.author: NeuroLinea Focus Drills (AI-drafted, fact-checked; requires expert review)

questions.stem: A patient for cEEG has a right craniotomy. How should the electrodes be placed?
options: Leave the whole right hemisphere unrecorded
Use needle electrodes over the defect
Place electrodes over the bone flap as usual
Move the left homologue to match; note the defect
questions.explanation: Use at least 16 electrodes, note skull defects, drains and bolts, and when an electrode must be moved, move its homologue symmetrically so the hemispheres can still be compared. Over a skull defect, a breach effect (higher-amplitude, sharper, faster activity) is expected and its location should be given.
questions.memoryAid: MOVE ONE, MOVE ITS TWIN: keep left and right comparable.
questions.author: NeuroLinea Focus Drills (AI-drafted, fact-checked; requires expert review)

questions.stem: Which feature is required for a posterior rhythm to count as the posterior dominant rhythm (PDR)?
options: It is maximal over the vertex
questions.explanation: The PDR is a sinusoidal, symmetric rhythm maximal posteriorly in relaxed wakefulness with eyes closed, 8 to 13 Hz in adults (slower in young children), and it must attenuate with eye opening. A posterior rhythm that does not react is not called a PDR, and poor reactivity can be significant in context.
questions.memoryAid: PDR = Posterior, Drowsy-eyes-shut, Reacts to eyes opening.
questions.author: NeuroLinea Focus Drills (AI-drafted, fact-checked; requires expert review)

questions.stem: Rhythmic 11 to 15 Hz bursts lasting 0.5 to 2 seconds, maximal centrally in N2 sleep, are what?
questions.explanation: Sleep spindles are 11 to 15 Hz rhythmic bursts of 0.5 to 2 s, maximal centrally and frontally, in N2 and N3. They are a normal sleep element; mu is awake and blocks with movement, and drug beta is faster (18 to 25 Hz) and more continuous.
questions.memoryAid: SPINDLES spin for a SECOND at about 12-14 Hz in N2.
questions.author: NeuroLinea Focus Drills (AI-drafted, fact-checked; requires expert review)

questions.stem: In N2 sleep, a high-amplitude sharp negative wave followed by a positive wave, maximal frontocentrally, is what?
questions.explanation: A K-complex is a sharp negative wave followed by a positive wave, maximal frontally and centrally, spontaneous or evoked by a sound, and a marker of N2. It is broader and larger than a vertex sharp wave and has no after-going slow wave of a spike-and-wave.
questions.memoryAid: K-complex = a big frontal 'K' kick, often after a noise, in N2.
questions.author: NeuroLinea Focus Drills (AI-drafted, fact-checked; requires expert review)

questions.stem: Which finding marks REM sleep on the EEG?
options: Sawtooth waves with rapid eye movements
questions.explanation: REM shows a low-voltage mixed-frequency background like drowsiness, rapid conjugate eye movements (opposite polarity at F7 and F8), notched 2 to 6 Hz sawtooth waves maximal centrally, and loss of chin EMG tone. Spindles, K-complexes and vertex waves are absent. Sleep-onset REM on a routine EEG is reportable.
questions.memoryAid: REM = Rapid eyes, sawtooth on the vertex, no spindles.
questions.author: NeuroLinea Focus Drills (AI-drafted, fact-checked; requires expert review)

questions.stem: During photic stimulation, posterior waves follow each flash at the flash rate and stop when the flashes stop. What is this?
questions.explanation: Photic driving is posterior activity time-locked to each flash at the flash rate or a harmonic, present only during the train. It is normal, and its absence is not abnormal; marked persistent asymmetry may suggest a lesion on the side with the lower response.
questions.memoryAid: DRIVING follows the flash like a car follows the road.
questions.author: NeuroLinea Focus Drills (AI-drafted, fact-checked; requires expert review)

questions.stem: In a child, where is the hyperventilation build-up usually maximal, and when should it resolve?
options: Posteriorly; within about 1 minute of stopping
questions.explanation: HV build-up is diffuse rhythmic delta or theta that grows during HV: posterior maximum in children, frontal in adolescents and adults. It resolves within about 1 minute of stopping and is enhanced by hypoglycaemia. Asymmetry, spikes or persistence afterwards are reportable.
questions.memoryAid: Kids build at the BACK, adults at the FRONT; gone within a minute.
questions.author: NeuroLinea Focus Drills (AI-drafted, fact-checked; requires expert review)

questions.stem: An arch-shaped 8 to 10 Hz rhythm at C3 blocks when the patient moves the right hand. What is it?
questions.explanation: Mu is a central (C3, C4, Cz) arch-shaped 8 to 10 Hz rhythm that blocks with movement, or intention to move, of the opposite limb. It is a normal variant with no after-going slow wave.
questions.memoryAid: MU = Move yoUr hand and it stops.
questions.author: NeuroLinea Focus Drills (AI-drafted, fact-checked; requires expert review)

questions.stem: Trains of monophasic arciform 6 to 11 Hz waves over the left temporal region in drowsiness, with no after-going slow wave, are what?
questions.explanation: Wicket spikes occur in trains (or singly) over the temporal regions, left more than right or shifting, in wakefulness, drowsiness and light sleep, and vanish in deep sleep. They lack after-going slow waves and do not disrupt the background. A single one should be compared with a train elsewhere.
questions.memoryAid: WICKETS come in a ROW, like a cricket wicket, with no slow wave behind.
questions.author: NeuroLinea Focus Drills (AI-drafted, fact-checked; requires expert review)

questions.stem: Sharp, triangular, positive occipital waves appear while an awake patient reads and vanish with eye closure. What are they?
questions.explanation: Lambda waves are positive occipital sharp transients during visual scanning and disappear when the eyes close. POSTS look similar but occur in sleep. The reactivity to vision distinguishes them from epileptiform activity.
questions.memoryAid: LAMBDA = Looking. POSTS = Sleeping.
questions.author: NeuroLinea Focus Drills (AI-drafted, fact-checked; requires expert review)

questions.stem: Positive sharp transients at O1 and O2 during N2 sleep in an adult are most likely what?
questions.explanation: Positive occipital sharp transients of sleep (POSTS) are positive, triangular, occipital, often bilateral, seen in N2 and N3. They are normal; their positive polarity and sleep state separate them from occipital spikes.
questions.memoryAid: POSTS = Positive Occipital Sharp Transients of Sleep: the name says it all.
questions.author: NeuroLinea Focus Drills (AI-drafted, fact-checked; requires expert review)

questions.stem: Notched rhythmic 5 to 7 Hz theta, maximal mid-temporally with shifting sides in drowsiness, that never evolves, is what?
questions.explanation: Rhythmic mid-temporal theta of drowsiness (RMTD, psychomotor variant) is monomorphic and monorhythmic, often notched, bilateral with shifting emphasis, in relaxed wakefulness and drowsiness. It does not evolve, which separates it from a seizure.
questions.memoryAid: RMTD: Rhythmic, Mid-Temporal, Drowsy, and it never changes.
questions.author: NeuroLinea Focus Drills (AI-drafted, fact-checked; requires expert review)

questions.stem: Low-voltage (under 50 µV), very brief (under 50 ms) temporal spikes in an adult's light sleep, single and without a slow wave, are what?
questions.explanation: Benign epileptiform transients of sleep (BETS, small sharp spikes) are under 50 µV and under 50 ms, mono- or diphasic, single rather than in trains, in drowsiness and light sleep, often independent on each side. They disappear in deeper sleep and lack after-going slow waves.
questions.memoryAid: BETS are SMALL and SHORT: under 50 and under 50.
questions.author: NeuroLinea Focus Drills (AI-drafted, fact-checked; requires expert review)

questions.stem: Sharp waves maximal at Cz during light sleep in a child are most likely what?
questions.explanation: Vertex sharp waves are normal sleep elements maximal at Cz, often prominent and sharp in children, and may be asymmetric. They mark drowsiness and N1 to N2.
questions.memoryAid: VERTEX = top of the head, top of sleep (N1-N2).
questions.author: NeuroLinea Focus Drills (AI-drafted, fact-checked; requires expert review)

questions.stem: A notched posterior rhythm runs at exactly twice the patient's alpha frequency and blocks with eye opening. What is it?
questions.explanation: The fast alpha variant is a harmonic of the PDR at twice its frequency (16 to 26 Hz), notched, posterior and reactive to eye opening. Ordinary beta is frontocentral and does not share the alpha's reactivity.
questions.memoryAid: FAST alpha = DOUBLE the alpha, still at the back.
questions.author: NeuroLinea Focus Drills (AI-drafted, fact-checked; requires expert review)

questions.stem: A notched 4.5 Hz posterior rhythm appears at half the alpha frequency and blocks with eye opening. What is the key to calling it a normal variant?
options: Its reactivity to eye opening, like alpha
Its presence only in deep sleep
A slow wave after each notch
Its location over the temporal lobes
questions.explanation: The slow alpha variant is a subharmonic at half the PDR (4 to 6.5 Hz), posterior and notched. Reactivity to eye opening and closing is the key; without it, it can be hard to tell from pathological slowing.
questions.memoryAid: SLOW alpha = HALF the alpha; prove it by opening the eyes.
questions.author: NeuroLinea Focus Drills (AI-drafted, fact-checked; requires expert review)

questions.stem: How should alpha squeak be handled when measuring the PDR?
options: Measure the PDR only while it lasts
Use it as the true PDR frequency
Report it as an abnormal finding
Skip the first 0.5-1 s after eye closure
questions.explanation: Alpha squeak is a brief rise in alpha frequency right after eye closure. Measuring the PDR during it overestimates the frequency, so the first 0.5 to 1 s after closure is skipped.
questions.memoryAid: The alpha SQUEAKS when the eyes shut: wait a second, then measure.
questions.author: NeuroLinea Focus Drills (AI-drafted, fact-checked; requires expert review)

questions.stem: Rhythmic 5 to 7 Hz activity maximal at Cz in an awake adult, with variable reactivity, is most likely what?
questions.explanation: Midline theta (Ciganek rhythm) is 5 to 7 Hz, most prominent at Cz, smooth, arciform or spiky, with variable reactivity, in wakefulness and drowsiness. Mu is faster (8 to 10 Hz) and blocks with movement.
questions.memoryAid: CIGANEK sits in the MIDDLE (Cz) at theta speed.
questions.author: NeuroLinea Focus Drills (AI-drafted, fact-checked; requires expert review)

questions.stem: A 62-year-old has an abrupt-onset rhythmic 5 to 7 Hz pattern with a parietal maximum for 2 minutes during HV, with no clinical change. What is it most likely?
questions.explanation: Subclinical rhythmic electrographic discharge of adults (SREDA) occurs over age 50, begins abruptly with mixed delta and theta that becomes rhythmic 5 to 7 Hz, lasts 20 s to a few minutes, is maximal parietally and posterior temporally, and usually has no clinical correlate (though this is debated).
questions.memoryAid: SREDA = Seniors, Rhythmic, Evolves, Does no harm (usually), Abrupt.
questions.author: NeuroLinea Focus Drills (AI-drafted, fact-checked; requires expert review)

questions.stem: A 13-year-old in light sleep has arch-shaped bursts with positive spiky components, maximal posterior-temporally. Which montage shows them best?
questions.explanation: 14 and 6 Hz positive bursts (ctenoids) peak at ages 13 to 14, occur in drowsiness and light sleep, are maximal posterior-temporally with shifting sides, and are best seen with long interelectrode distances in referential (ear) montages. They may be enhanced in Reye syndrome.
questions.memoryAid: 14 and 6 at age 14: look with the EARS (ear reference).
questions.author: NeuroLinea Focus Drills (AI-drafted, fact-checked; requires expert review)

questions.stem: Which type of 6 Hz spike-and-wave (phantom spike-and-wave) is more likely to be linked with seizures?
options: Any type that vanishes in deep sleep
questions.explanation: Phantom spike-and-wave is brief 5 to 7 Hz bursts of tiny spikes with a more obvious slow wave, in relaxed wakefulness and drowsiness, gone in deep sleep. FOLD is benign; WHAM is more often associated with seizures.
questions.memoryAid: FOLD is fine; WHAM can hit hard.
questions.author: NeuroLinea Focus Drills (AI-drafted, fact-checked; requires expert review)

questions.stem: A 3-year-old drifting off to sleep has bursts of high-voltage rhythmic 3 to 5 Hz waves without spikes. What is this?
questions.explanation: Hypnagogic hypersynchrony is normal in infants and children (about 3 months to 13 years, most prominent at 1 to 5): bursts of high-voltage rhythmic 3 to 5 Hz waves at the onset of drowsiness that disappear in deeper sleep and on arousal. True embedded spikes or bursts in full wakefulness would be concerning.
questions.memoryAid: HYPNAGOGIC = sleepy-onset hello wave in toddlers, no spikes.
questions.author: NeuroLinea Focus Drills (AI-drafted, fact-checked; requires expert review)

questions.stem: An awake 11-year-old has single delta waves fused with the posterior alpha that block with eye opening. What are they?
questions.explanation: Posterior slow waves of youth are single 2.5 to 4.5 Hz delta waves with the alpha riding on them, bilateral (sometimes asymmetric), most common at 8 to 14 and rare after 21. They share the alpha's reactivity and disappear in sleep.
questions.memoryAid: YOUTH waves ride WITH the alpha and BLOCK with it.
questions.author: NeuroLinea Focus Drills (AI-drafted, fact-checked; requires expert review)

questions.stem: After a right craniotomy, higher-amplitude, sharper, faster activity appears over the right central region with no slow waves or evolution. What is it?
questions.explanation: A breach rhythm is higher-amplitude (up to three times), sharper, arciform, mu-like activity with more beta over a skull defect, because bone normally attenuates the EEG. It is not epileptiform by itself; document the skull defect.
questions.memoryAid: A HOLE in the bone lets the brain SHOUT louder.
questions.author: NeuroLinea Focus Drills (AI-drafted, fact-checked; requires expert review)

questions.stem: Which feature best separates a true temporal spike from a benign variant such as a wicket?
options: A frequency of 6 to 11 Hz in trains
A slow wave after it that disrupts the background
Appearing only in drowsiness or light sleep
Positive polarity at the scalp surface
questions.explanation: Epileptiform spikes are followed by a slow wave and disrupt the background; benign variants such as wickets and BETS lack both. Focal temporal spikes are associated with temporal lobe epilepsy and are seen awake and asleep.
questions.memoryAid: A real spike drags a SLOW WAVE behind it and DISTURBS the background.
questions.author: NeuroLinea Focus Drills (AI-drafted, fact-checked; requires expert review)

questions.stem: Frontal spikes in a frontal lobe epilepsy patient are best brought out by what?
questions.explanation: Frontal spikes have after-going slow waves, may disrupt the background and are enhanced by sleep, so a sleep recording raises the yield.
questions.memoryAid: Frontal spikes WAKE UP when the patient SLEEPS.
questions.author: NeuroLinea Focus Drills (AI-drafted, fact-checked; requires expert review)

questions.stem: A 7-year-old's staring spell coincides with generalized spike-and-wave of abrupt onset and offset. What frequency is typical, and what provokes it?
questions.explanation: Typical absence seizures show 3 Hz generalized spike-and-wave, frontally predominant, with abrupt onset and offset, provoked by hyperventilation, in childhood and juvenile absence epilepsy.
questions.memoryAid: ABSENCE = 3 Hz, and HV calls it out.
questions.author: NeuroLinea Focus Drills (AI-drafted, fact-checked; requires expert review)

questions.stem: A 4-year-old with tonic seizures has generalized spike-and-wave at 2 Hz, most prominent in sleep. What is it?
questions.explanation: Slow spike-and-wave at 1.5 to 2.5 Hz, generalized and sometimes asymmetric, is characteristic of Lennox-Gastaut syndrome (onset 1 to 8 years). It is most prominent in sleep, so a sleep recording is important.
questions.memoryAid: LGS is SLOW: under 3 Hz, and worse asleep.
questions.author: NeuroLinea Focus Drills (AI-drafted, fact-checked; requires expert review)

questions.stem: During sleep in a child with Lennox-Gastaut syndrome, generalized bursts of 20 to 50 Hz activity appear. What are they?
questions.explanation: GPFA is paroxysmal generalized fast activity (20 to 50 Hz) in sleep, highly characteristic of LGS and often associated with tonic seizures.
questions.memoryAid: GPFA = Lennox's FAST signature during sleep, with tonic seizures.
questions.author: NeuroLinea Focus Drills (AI-drafted, fact-checked; requires expert review)

questions.stem: A teenager with morning myoclonic jerks has generalized discharges of several spikes followed by a slow wave. What is the pattern, and what activates it?
questions.explanation: Polyspike-and-wave (2 to 5 or more spikes then a slow wave), generalized and symmetric, is typical of juvenile myoclonic epilepsy and is activated by sleep deprivation and awakening.
questions.memoryAid: JME = many SPIKES in the MORNING after a short night.
questions.author: NeuroLinea Focus Drills (AI-drafted, fact-checked; requires expert review)

questions.stem: Chaotic, very high-amplitude slow waves with multifocal spikes in a 6-month-old with spasms is called what?
questions.explanation: Hypsarrhythmia is the interictal pattern of West syndrome: chaotic, high-amplitude slow waves with multifocal spikes. Spasms need urgent treatment (ACTH or steroids, vigabatrin especially in tuberous sclerosis); success means the spasms stop and the hypsarrhythmia resolves.
questions.memoryAid: HYPS = HIGH and CHAOTIC, with spikes everywhere.
questions.author: NeuroLinea Focus Drills (AI-drafted, fact-checked; requires expert review)

questions.stem: In a school-age child, where are centrotemporal spikes maximal and what dipole do they show?
options: Cz; radial, negative at the vertex
questions.explanation: Centrotemporal spikes of SeLECTS are high-amplitude diphasic spikes with a slow wave, maximal at central and mid-temporal electrodes, with a tangential dipole (negative centrotemporally, positive frontally), on a normal background and markedly activated by sleep.
questions.memoryAid: ROLANDIC spikes lie SIDEWAYS: negative at the side, positive in front.
questions.author: NeuroLinea Focus Drills (AI-drafted, fact-checked; requires expert review)

questions.stem: Generalized spike-and-wave appears during photic stimulation at 16 flashes/s. What should the technologist do first?
questions.explanation: A photoparoxysmal response is generalized spike or polyspike-and-wave provoked by photic stimulation, not time-locked to the flashes, most often at 14 to 20 Hz, and linked with genetic generalized epilepsies. Stop the stimulation as soon as it appears and record the provoking rates and whether it outlasted the stimulus.
questions.memoryAid: Spikes in the strobe? STOP the strobe.
questions.author: NeuroLinea Focus Drills (AI-drafted, fact-checked; requires expert review)

questions.stem: Runs of sinusoidal 1 to 3 Hz delta confined to one anterior temporal region, on a normal background, carry what significance?
options: None; it is a normal variant
questions.explanation: Temporal intermittent rhythmic delta activity (TIRDA) is rhythmic sinusoidal delta at F7/T3 or F8/T4 and carries the same epileptogenic significance as temporal spikes, often with mesial temporal sclerosis. It is rhythmic, unlike the polymorphic delta of a structural lesion.
questions.memoryAid: TIRDA = a temporal SPIKE in disguise.
questions.author: NeuroLinea Focus Drills (AI-drafted, fact-checked; requires expert review)

questions.stem: A child has unilateral focal slowing and spikes on the side of a facial port-wine stain. Which condition fits?
questions.explanation: In Sturge-Weber syndrome the EEG shows unilateral focal slowing, spikes and background asymmetry on the side of the leptomeningeal angioma, with a port-wine stain (V1) from birth and seizures beginning in infancy.
questions.memoryAid: PORT-WINE stain → abnormal EEG on the SAME side.
questions.author: NeuroLinea Focus Drills (AI-drafted, fact-checked; requires expert review)

questions.stem: Bilateral spike-and-wave is always preceded by a left frontal spike and stays larger on the left. What does this suggest?
questions.explanation: A consistent focal lead-in and persistent asymmetry suggest secondary bilateral synchrony: a focal (often mesial frontal) discharge spreading rapidly across the corpus callosum. Describe the lead-in and asymmetry; ACNS 2021 calls such a pattern lateralized.
questions.memoryAid: A LEAD-IN from one side means it STARTED on that side.
questions.author: NeuroLinea Focus Drills (AI-drafted, fact-checked; requires expert review)

questions.stem: A child with prior measles has huge stereotyped generalized complexes every 4 to 15 seconds with myoclonic jerks. What is it?
questions.explanation: Subacute sclerosing panencephalitis shows very high-amplitude stereotyped generalized complexes at long, regular intervals (usually 4 to 15 s), often time-locked to myoclonic jerks, on a progressively slow background. CJD complexes repeat about once a second.
questions.memoryAid: SSPE = Slow Spacing (4-15 s). CJD = about every second.
questions.author: NeuroLinea Focus Drills (AI-drafted, fact-checked; requires expert review)

questions.stem: A 64-year-old with dementia progressing over weeks and startle myoclonus has bilateral synchronous sharp waves at about 1 Hz. What do they suggest?
questions.explanation: Periodic sharp wave complexes at 0.5 to 2 Hz (typically about 1 Hz), bilateral and synchronous, are highly characteristic of CJD, with rapidly progressive dementia and stimulus-sensitive myoclonus. They may be absent early, so their absence does not exclude CJD.
questions.memoryAid: CJD = 1 per second, and a mind failing in WEEKS.
questions.author: NeuroLinea Focus Drills (AI-drafted, fact-checked; requires expert review)

questions.stem: Periodic sharp waves at 1 Hz over the left hemisphere only, in a patient with acute stroke, are called what?
questions.explanation: Lateralized periodic discharges are sharp waves or spikes recurring at regular intervals (typically 0.5 to 2 Hz) over one hemisphere, indicating acute or subacute focal cortical dysfunction: most often stroke, also herpes encephalitis, tumour and trauma. They may be ictal or interictal; notify the team.
questions.memoryAid: L-P-D = Lesion on one side, Periodic, Discharges.
questions.author: NeuroLinea Focus Drills (AI-drafted, fact-checked; requires expert review)

questions.stem: Bilateral symmetric theta and delta persisting in alert wakefulness indicates what?
questions.explanation: Diffuse slowing is bilateral and symmetric and persists when the patient is fully alert, which separates it from drowsy slowing. It indicates generalized dysfunction such as metabolic or toxic encephalopathy.
questions.memoryAid: Slow while ALERT = the whole brain is struggling.
questions.author: NeuroLinea Focus Drills (AI-drafted, fact-checked; requires expert review)

questions.stem: Irregular delta confined to one region that persists across all states most likely indicates what?
questions.explanation: Focal slowing is regional and persists across states, unlike drowsy slowing, and indicates focal cortical dysfunction, usually a structural lesion. Polymorphic (irregular) delta points to structure; rhythmic delta has other meanings.
questions.memoryAid: STAYS in one place and STAYS in every state = a lesion.
questions.author: NeuroLinea Focus Drills (AI-drafted, fact-checked; requires expert review)

questions.stem: Intermittent rhythmic 1 to 3 Hz delta, frontally predominant, in an encephalopathic adult is now called what?
questions.explanation: FIRDA (frontal intermittent rhythmic delta activity) is renamed frontally predominant GRDA in the 2021 terminology. It is seen in encephalopathy and is distinct from irregular pathological slowing.
questions.memoryAid: FIRDA is now GRDA with a FRONT seat.
questions.author: NeuroLinea Focus Drills (AI-drafted, fact-checked; requires expert review)

questions.stem: Intermittent rhythmic delta over the occipital regions is more common in which age group?
questions.explanation: Occipital intermittent rhythmic delta activity (OIRDA) is rhythmic posterior delta, more common in children than adults, and is seen in encephalopathy and with generalized epilepsies such as absence.
questions.memoryAid: OIRDA = Occipital In the young; FIRDA = Front in adults.
questions.author: NeuroLinea Focus Drills (AI-drafted, fact-checked; requires expert review)

questions.stem: Generalized frontally predominant negative-positive-negative waves at about 2 Hz in a jaundiced, confused patient suggest what?
questions.explanation: Triphasic waves (now GPDs with triphasic morphology) are three-phase, frontally predominant, about 1.5 to 2.5 Hz and often reactive to stimulation. They are highly characteristic of hepatic encephalopathy but also occur in uraemia, hyperglycaemia and lithium toxicity.
questions.memoryAid: TRI-phasic = three phases, think LIVER first.
questions.author: NeuroLinea Focus Drills (AI-drafted, fact-checked; requires expert review)

questions.stem: After cardiac arrest, the EEG alternates bursts of mixed activity with flat periods. What is this, and what does persistence mean?
questions.explanation: Burst suppression alternates bursts of mixed frequencies with flat or near-flat suppression. It indicates severe cortical dysfunction (anoxia, deep anaesthesia, severe metabolic or toxic states); a persistent pattern after anoxia carries a poor prognosis.
questions.memoryAid: BURST then FLAT, BURST then FLAT = a brain barely holding on.
questions.author: NeuroLinea Focus Drills (AI-drafted, fact-checked; requires expert review)

questions.stem: A comatose patient after cardiac arrest has widespread 10 Hz activity that does not change with stimulation. What is this?
questions.explanation: Alpha coma is generalized, non-reactive alpha-frequency activity in a comatose patient, linked with severe hypoxic or brainstem injury and a very poor prognosis. A normal PDR is posterior and reactive.
questions.memoryAid: ALPHA in a COMA that does not REACT = bad news.
questions.author: NeuroLinea Focus Drills (AI-drafted, fact-checked; requires expert review)

questions.stem: A young woman with psychiatric symptoms, dyskinesias and seizures has rhythmic delta with superimposed 20 to 30 Hz beta. What is it, and what does it suggest?
options: Delta brushes of prematurity; normal finding
questions.explanation: Extreme delta brush (rhythmic 1 to 3 Hz delta with superimposed beta) is characteristic of anti-NMDA receptor encephalitis. In the 2021 terminology it is a subtype of the +F modifier.
questions.memoryAid: EXTREME delta brush = NMDA: young, psychiatric, moving, seizing.
questions.author: NeuroLinea Focus Drills (AI-drafted, fact-checked; requires expert review)

questions.stem: What is required to report electrocerebral inactivity (ECI)?
options: No activity over 10 µV at 7 µV/mm
Alpha activity that does not react
No cerebral activity over 2 µV at 2 µV/mm
questions.explanation: ECI is no electrocerebral activity over 2 µV at a sensitivity of 2 µV/mm, with double-distance electrodes, for at least 30 minutes, impedances 100 to 10,000 Ω, reactivity testing and a touch test. Remaining waveforms (EKG, ventilator) must be identified as artifact; drug intoxication and hypothermia must be excluded.
questions.memoryAid: ECI = nothing over 2 µV at 2 µV/mm.
questions.author: NeuroLinea Focus Drills (AI-drafted, fact-checked; requires expert review)

questions.stem: What defines a focal electrographic seizure arising from the temporal lobe?
options: Slowing that stays unchanged for an hour
Rhythm that evolves in speed, size and spread
A single high-amplitude spike with slow wave
Notched theta in drowsiness that never evolves
questions.explanation: A focal seizure shows abrupt rhythmic activity distinct from the background that evolves in frequency (often faster to slower), amplitude (rising) and field (spreading), sometimes starting with attenuation or low-voltage fast activity, often with post-ictal slowing. Notify per protocol and test responsiveness.
questions.memoryAid: A SEIZURE CHANGES: speed, size and spread.
questions.author: NeuroLinea Focus Drills (AI-drafted, fact-checked; requires expert review)

questions.stem: During an infantile spasm, what is the typical ictal EEG correlate?
options: A big slow wave, then diffuse attenuation
An evolving focal theta rhythm over C3
questions.explanation: The electrodecremental event: a generalized high-amplitude slow transient followed by abrupt diffuse attenuation for one to several seconds, often with low-amplitude fast activity, on a hypsarrhythmic background, time-locked to the spasm. Video and deltoid EMG help confirm it.
questions.memoryAid: A SPASM = a big wave, then the background goes QUIET.
questions.author: NeuroLinea Focus Drills (AI-drafted, fact-checked; requires expert review)

questions.stem: Which statement about neonatal electrographic seizures is correct?
options: Need only 2 s of rhythmic activity
Always seen with visible clinical jerking
Mostly focal, often silent, 10 s or more
questions.explanation: Neonatal seizures are mostly focal (often central or temporal), evolve in frequency, amplitude, morphology or field, last at least 10 s, and are frequently electrographic only. Generalized 3 Hz spike-and-wave does not occur in newborns, so continuous EEG is needed.
questions.memoryAid: NEWBORN seizures: FOCAL, SILENT, 10 seconds or more.
questions.author: NeuroLinea Focus Drills (AI-drafted, fact-checked; requires expert review)

questions.stem: During a blink, why do Fp1 and Fp2 become positive?
options: The positive cornea rolls up under the eyelid
The negative retina moves toward the forehead
questions.explanation: The cornea is positive relative to the retina. During a blink the eyes roll up (Bell phenomenon), bringing the cornea toward Fp1/Fp2, so they become positive: a downward deflection in Fp1-F3 and Fp1-F7. The field falls off quickly behind the frontal poles.
questions.memoryAid: CORNEA is a PLUS sign; blink = eyes UP = Fp goes positive.
questions.author: NeuroLinea Focus Drills (AI-drafted, fact-checked; requires expert review)

questions.stem: A patient looks to the left. What happens at F7 and F8?
options: F7 becomes negative and F8 positive
F7 becomes positive and F8 negative
questions.explanation: The eye turning toward an electrode brings its positive cornea near it. Looking left, F7 becomes positive and F8 negative, so the two temporal chains deflect in opposite directions; lateral rectus spikes may appear at the start of the saccade.
questions.memoryAid: LOOK LEFT, LEFT goes POSITIVE (F7).
questions.author: NeuroLinea Focus Drills (AI-drafted, fact-checked; requires expert review)

questions.stem: Very fast spiky activity over 20 Hz in dense runs over the temporal regions during jaw clenching is what?
questions.explanation: Muscle artifact is dense, very short (under 20 ms) spiky potentials over the temporalis and frontalis, gone with relaxation or sleep. Lowering the HFF reduces but does not remove it, and over-filtering can make it look like cerebral beta. It can hide seizures.
questions.memoryAid: CLENCH = TEMPORAL BUZZ. Relax the jaw, not the filter.
questions.author: NeuroLinea Focus Drills (AI-drafted, fact-checked; requires expert review)

questions.stem: A steep deflection with a slow exponential return appears only in channels containing T4, with no field around it. What is it?
questions.explanation: Electrode pop is an abrupt change in impedance at one electrode (drying gel, loose contact): a sudden steep deflection with exponential decay, confined to that electrode's channels with no surrounding field. Re-gel or re-apply the electrode.
questions.memoryAid: ONE electrode, NO field = a POP, not the brain.
questions.author: NeuroLinea Focus Drills (AI-drafted, fact-checked; requires expert review)

questions.stem: A perfectly regular 60 Hz band appears in every channel. What should be suspected first?
options: A poor ground or the environment
questions.explanation: 60 Hz interference is monotonous and exactly at mains frequency. In a few channels it points to one high- or unequal-impedance electrode; in all channels, suspect the ground or nearby equipment. The notch removes it but can hide a bad electrode.
questions.memoryAid: 60 Hz in ONE = bad electrode; in ALL = bad ground.
questions.author: NeuroLinea Focus Drills (AI-drafted, fact-checked; requires expert review)

questions.stem: Small sharp transients in the left temporal and ear-referenced channels line up exactly with each R wave. What are they?
questions.explanation: EKG artifact coincides with the QRS complex, is most prominent in ear-referenced and left temporal channels, is regular at the heart rate and can mimic periodic sharp waves. Always record an EKG channel to identify it.
questions.memoryAid: ON the R wave = EKG. AFTER it = pulse.
questions.author: NeuroLinea Focus Drills (AI-drafted, fact-checked; requires expert review)

questions.stem: A smooth slow wave at one electrode recurs about 250 ms after each QRS. What is it, and how is it fixed?
options: Focal slow wave; report it as such
EKG artifact; switch to linked ears
Sweat artifact; raise the LFF to 5 Hz
questions.explanation: Pulse artifact is mechanical: the electrode moves over a pulsating artery, giving a slow or triangular wave a fixed delay (about 200 to 300 ms) after each QRS. Moving the electrode slightly removes it. EKG artifact, by contrast, coincides with the QRS.
questions.memoryAid: PULSE comes a beat LATE; move the electrode off the artery.
questions.author: NeuroLinea Focus Drills (AI-drafted, fact-checked; requires expert review)

questions.stem: Broad delta-like waves appear over frontal and temporal regions whenever the patient talks. How can the technologist confirm the cause?
options: Ask the patient to look left
Ask the patient to clench the jaw
Ask the patient to say 'la la la'
questions.explanation: Glossokinetic artifact comes from the tongue (tip negative relative to base): broad slow waves with talking, chewing or swallowing, in phase on both sides, gone when the tongue is still. Repeating 'la la la' reproduces it.
questions.memoryAid: TONGUE waves: make them say LA LA LA.
questions.author: NeuroLinea Focus Drills (AI-drafted, fact-checked; requires expert review)

questions.stem: Very slow (under 0.5 Hz) high-amplitude sways at a few forehead electrodes in a warm room are most likely what?
questions.explanation: Sweat changes the electrode-skin potential, producing very slow baseline sways with a period of 2 s or longer at a few electrodes. A higher LFF reduces it, but the patient should be cooled; severe sweat can bridge electrodes.
questions.memoryAid: SLOW SWAY + WARM room = SWEAT. Cool the patient.
questions.author: NeuroLinea Focus Drills (AI-drafted, fact-checked; requires expert review)

questions.stem: Brief muscle spikes at Fp1, Fp2, F7 and F8 follow each photic flash by about 50 ms and stop as soon as the flashes stop. What is this?
questions.explanation: The photomyogenic (photomyoclonic) response is frontal muscle activity time-locked to each flash, often with visible eyelid or facial twitching, ending when stimulation ends. It is muscle, not epileptiform; it is commoner with anxiety and alcohol or drug withdrawal.
questions.memoryAid: MYO = MUSCLE at the FRONT, locked to each flash.
questions.author: NeuroLinea Focus Drills (AI-drafted, fact-checked; requires expert review)

questions.stem: One channel between two adjacent electrodes is nearly flat while its neighbours look normal. What is the likely cause?
options: A focal suppression from a lesion
A salt bridge between the two electrodes
questions.explanation: A salt bridge (sweat, gel or paste joining two electrodes) makes both record the same potential, so the channel between them is nearly isoelectric. The impedance check shows low impedance between them; clean and re-apply.
questions.memoryAid: A FLAT channel between two neighbours = they are BRIDGED.
questions.author: NeuroLinea Focus Drills (AI-drafted, fact-checked; requires expert review)

questions.stem: Rhythmic bursts of muscle activity over both temporal regions, about one per second, appear during a temporal lobe seizure. Why must the technologist look carefully?
options: Chewing automatisms can hide the ictal pattern
Chewing proves the event is not a seizure
questions.explanation: Chewing artifact is regular bursts of temporalis muscle activity at the chewing rate with a clean background between bursts. Chewing during an event may be an automatism of a temporal lobe seizure, and the muscle can mask the ictal rhythm underneath.
questions.memoryAid: CHEWING in an event: look UNDER the muscle for the seizure.
questions.author: NeuroLinea Focus Drills (AI-drafted, fact-checked; requires expert review)

questions.stem: Abundant 18 to 25 Hz frontocentral beta over 25 µV in a patient on lorazepam is what, and what does a focal loss of it suggest?
options: A drug effect; lesion on the low side
questions.explanation: Excess beta is the commonest medication effect on the EEG (benzodiazepines, barbiturates, chloral hydrate), usually frontocentral or diffuse, often more prominent in drowsiness. Beta that is reduced on one side points to an abnormality, such as a lesion or fluid collection, on that side.
questions.memoryAid: BENZO = BETA. Less beta on one side = trouble on that side.
questions.author: NeuroLinea Focus Drills (AI-drafted, fact-checked; requires expert review)

questions.stem: A neonate at 27 weeks postmenstrual age has bursts separated by long very low-voltage intervals in all states. How is this interpreted?
options: Tracé alternant of a term infant
Tracé discontinu, normal for the age
questions.explanation: Tracé discontinu is the normal discontinuous background of prematurity: bursts with delta brushes, temporal theta and sharp transients separated by very low-voltage intervals. The longest normal interburst interval shortens with age, so always judge against postmenstrual age.
questions.memoryAid: PREMATURE = DIScontinuous is OK; check the gaps for age.
questions.author: NeuroLinea Focus Drills (AI-drafted, fact-checked; requires expert review)

questions.stem: In which state is tracé alternant normally seen in a term newborn?
questions.explanation: Tracé alternant is the normal quiet-sleep pattern of term and near-term newborns (about 37 to 44 weeks): 3 to 8 s bursts alternating with lower-voltage (not suppressed) segments. It is replaced by continuous slow-wave sleep by about 46 weeks.
questions.memoryAid: ALTERNANT = Quiet sleep at term: loud, soft, loud, soft.
questions.author: NeuroLinea Focus Drills (AI-drafted, fact-checked; requires expert review)

questions.stem: At what postmenstrual age are delta brushes most abundant?
questions.explanation: Delta brushes (0.5 to 1.5 Hz delta with superimposed 8 to 20 Hz fast activity) appear around 26 weeks, are most abundant at 32 to 34 weeks, decrease toward term and are gone by about 44 weeks. Persistence beyond term suggests dysmaturity.
questions.memoryAid: BRUSHES peak in the early 30s (weeks), gone by 44.
questions.author: NeuroLinea Focus Drills (AI-drafted, fact-checked; requires expert review)

questions.stem: Brief, sharply contoured 4 to 6 Hz runs over both temporal regions in a 28-week infant are what?
questions.explanation: Temporal theta of prematurity (temporal sawtooth) is a normal marker of early prematurity (about 26 to 30 weeks): short runs of sharply contoured theta, often asynchronous, embedded in the bursts. They disappear by about 32 to 33 weeks.
questions.memoryAid: TEMPORAL THETA = the very YOUNG preemie's signature.
questions.author: NeuroLinea Focus Drills (AI-drafted, fact-checked; requires expert review)

questions.stem: Broad, bilaterally synchronous diphasic frontal sharp transients in a term newborn's quiet sleep are what?
questions.explanation: Encoches frontales are normal frontal sharp transients of newborns (about 35 to 44 weeks), bilateral and synchronous, often with anterior slow dysrhythmia. A strictly one-sided frontal focus, or persistence beyond about 48 weeks, is not normal.
questions.memoryAid: ENCOCHES = 'notches' in the FRONT, on BOTH sides, in the newborn.
questions.author: NeuroLinea Focus Drills (AI-drafted, fact-checked; requires expert review)

questions.stem: Generalized, bilaterally synchronous periodic discharges at 2 Hz with a clear interval between them are what, under the 2021 terminology?
questions.explanation: GPDs are periodic discharges over both hemispheres, synchronous and symmetric, with an interval between them. Above 2.5 Hz for 10 s or more is an electrographic seizure; more than 1 and up to 2.5 Hz is on the IIC. GPDs replace the old GPEDs/PEDs.
questions.memoryAid: Count in 10 s: over 25 = seizure; 11-25 = IIC.
questions.author: NeuroLinea Focus Drills (AI-drafted, fact-checked; requires expert review)

questions.stem: Rhythmic 1.5 Hz delta with no gap between waves, consistently over the left hemisphere, is named what?
questions.explanation: Lateralized rhythmic delta activity is rhythmic delta (0.5 to 4 Hz) of uniform shape with no interval between waves, over one hemisphere, for at least 6 cycles. It is strongly associated with acute seizures, like LPDs; GRDA is never on the IIC, but LRDA can be.
questions.memoryAid: LRDA = left or right, rhythmic, no gaps, seizure risk.
questions.author: NeuroLinea Focus Drills (AI-drafted, fact-checked; requires expert review)

questions.stem: Periodic discharges run independently over each hemisphere at the same time in a comatose patient. What are they, and what do they imply?
questions.explanation: Bilateral independent periodic discharges are two independent lateralized periodic patterns, one in each hemisphere, at the same time (asynchronous, often at different rates). They replace BIPLEDs and are associated with more severe injury and coma than LPDs. Independent patterns at different times are two separate LPDs.
questions.memoryAid: BI = BOTH sides, INDEPENDENT, at the SAME time.
questions.author: NeuroLinea Focus Drills (AI-drafted, fact-checked; requires expert review)

questions.stem: A 6 Hz evolving rhythm lasting 4 seconds appears over T7 in an ICU patient with no clinical change. What is it?
questions.explanation: BIRDs are rhythmic activity over 4 Hz lasting 0.5 s to under 10 s, not a normal variant, with no clinical correlate. Evolution (or a match to the patient's seizures) makes them definite; sharp contour alone makes them possible. The same rhythm lasting 10 s or more is a seizure.
questions.memoryAid: FAST and BRIEF: over 4 Hz, under 10 s. Evolving = definite.
questions.author: NeuroLinea Focus Drills (AI-drafted, fact-checked; requires expert review)

questions.stem: Periodic discharges appear every time the nurse suctions a comatose patient. How should they be coded?
questions.explanation: Stimulus-induced patterns are reproducibly brought on by alerting stimuli (suctioning, exam, noise). Code the specific pattern with SI- (for example SI-GPDs), annotate the stimulus and its time, and report ictal-appearing SIRPIDs because they can be seizures.
questions.memoryAid: Suction brings it ON = SI-. Write what you did and when.
questions.author: NeuroLinea Focus Drills (AI-drafted, fact-checked; requires expert review)

questions.stem: LPDs run at about 2 Hz in a critically ill patient without definite seizure criteria. How is this classed?
questions.explanation: PDs or SW averaging more than 1 and up to 2.5 Hz over 10 s (more than 10 and up to 25 discharges) meet IIC criterion A, as long as seizure criteria are not met. IIC is an electrographic term (possible seizure), not a diagnosis; notify per protocol.
questions.memoryAid: 2 Hz LPDs sit on the FENCE between interictal and ictal.
questions.author: NeuroLinea Focus Drills (AI-drafted, fact-checked; requires expert review)

questions.stem: At a sensitivity of 7 µV/mm, a wave measures 8 mm from peak to trough. What is its amplitude?
questions.explanation: Amplitude = sensitivity × deflection: 7 µV/mm × 8 mm = 56 µV. The millimetres cancel and microvolts are left. Adding the numbers (15) or dividing them (0.9) are the usual slips; 112 doubles the answer for no reason.
questions.memoryAid: µV/mm × mm = µV. Let the units tell you to MULTIPLY.
questions.author: NeuroLinea Focus Drills (AI-drafted, fact-checked; requires expert review)

questions.stem: A 70 µV alpha rhythm is displayed at 10 µV/mm. How tall is it on the screen?
questions.explanation: Height = amplitude ÷ sensitivity: 70 µV ÷ 10 µV/mm = 7 mm. Multiplying gives an impossible 700 mm; the microvolts must cancel, which only happens when you divide.
questions.memoryAid: Going from µV to mm: DIVIDE by the µV/mm.
questions.author: NeuroLinea Focus Drills (AI-drafted, fact-checked; requires expert review)

questions.stem: A 50 µV calibration pulse produces a 10 mm deflection. What is the sensitivity?
questions.explanation: Sensitivity = µV ÷ mm: 50 ÷ 10 = 5 µV/mm. Each millimetre of pen travel stands for 5 microvolts. 0.2 is the answer upside down (mm per µV).
questions.memoryAid: Sensitivity reads as its units: µV PER mm, so µV ÷ mm.
questions.author: NeuroLinea Focus Drills (AI-drafted, fact-checked; requires expert review)

questions.stem: A wave is 10 mm tall at 7 µV/mm. The sensitivity is changed to 14 µV/mm. How tall is the same wave now?
questions.explanation: The wave is 70 µV (7 × 10). At 14 µV/mm it is 70 ÷ 14 = 5 mm. Doubling the µV/mm number halves the picture; the brain signal has not changed, only the display.
questions.memoryAid: Bigger µV/mm number = SMALLER picture. Double the number, halve the height.
questions.author: NeuroLinea Focus Drills (AI-drafted, fact-checked; requires expert review)

questions.stem: For an electrocerebral inactivity recording you want a 2 µV signal to show as a 1 mm deflection. What sensitivity is that?
questions.explanation: 2 µV ÷ 1 mm = 2 µV/mm, the sensitivity the ACNS protocol requires for ECI recordings, so that very low-voltage activity is not missed. 7 µV/mm is the routine setting.
questions.memoryAid: ECI: TWO µV per mm so you can see TOO little activity.
questions.author: NeuroLinea Focus Drills (AI-drafted, fact-checked; requires expert review)

questions.stem: At 10 µV/mm, a sharp wave rises 6 mm above the baseline and then falls 3 mm below it. What is its peak-to-peak amplitude?
questions.explanation: Peak to peak is the full excursion: 6 + 3 = 9 mm, and 9 × 10 = 90 µV. Using only the part above the baseline (60) or subtracting the two parts (30) under-measures it.
questions.memoryAid: Peak to peak = TOP to BOTTOM: add both sides of the baseline.
questions.author: NeuroLinea Focus Drills (AI-drafted, fact-checked; requires expert review)

questions.stem: At 30 mm/s, one complete wave spans 3 mm. What is its frequency?
questions.explanation: 3 mm at 30 mm/s lasts 3 ÷ 30 = 0.1 s, and 1 ÷ 0.1 = 10 Hz. Shortcut: at 30 mm/s, Hz = 30 ÷ wavelength in mm. 0.1 is the period in seconds, not the frequency.
questions.memoryAid: At 30 mm/s: Hz = 30 ÷ mm. Three-millimetre waves = TEN Hz alpha.
questions.author: NeuroLinea Focus Drills (AI-drafted, fact-checked; requires expert review)

questions.stem: At 30 mm/s, each wave in a run is 5 mm long. What frequency is the run, and what band?
questions.explanation: 30 ÷ 5 = 6 Hz, which is theta (4 to under 8 Hz). 5 Hz just reads the millimetres as hertz; 150 multiplies instead of dividing.
questions.memoryAid: Hz = 30 ÷ mm. Five-millimetre waves are six per second.
questions.author: NeuroLinea Focus Drills (AI-drafted, fact-checked; requires expert review)

questions.stem: At 30 mm/s, a transient is 3 mm wide at its base. How long does it last, and what is it called?
questions.explanation: At 30 mm/s each millimetre is about 33 ms, so 3 mm = 100 ms. Spikes last 20 to under 70 ms and sharp waves 70 to 200 ms, so 100 ms is a sharp wave.
questions.memoryAid: At 30 mm/s, 1 mm ≈ 33 ms, so 3 mm = 100 ms. SPIKE under 70, SHARP 70 to 200.
questions.author: NeuroLinea Focus Drills (AI-drafted, fact-checked; requires expert review)

questions.stem: At 30 mm/s, an epileptiform transient is 1.5 mm wide. How long is it, and what is it called?
questions.explanation: 1.5 mm × 33 ms ≈ 50 ms (or 1.5 ÷ 30 = 0.05 s). Under 70 ms makes it a spike. Reading 1.5 mm as 150 ms is a slip of the decimal point.
questions.memoryAid: Half of 3 mm (100 ms) is 1.5 mm (50 ms): under 70 = SPIKE.
questions.author: NeuroLinea Focus Drills (AI-drafted, fact-checked; requires expert review)

questions.stem: At 30 mm/s, periodic discharges recur every 45 mm. How often do they repeat?
questions.explanation: 45 mm ÷ 30 mm/s = 1.5 s between discharges, and 1 ÷ 1.5 ≈ 0.67 Hz. Writing the frequency as 1.5 Hz confuses the interval with the rate.
questions.memoryAid: Interval in seconds = mm ÷ 30. Rate = 1 ÷ interval.
questions.author: NeuroLinea Focus Drills (AI-drafted, fact-checked; requires expert review)

questions.stem: A neonatal EEG is displayed at 15 mm/s. A quiet interburst stretch measures 60 mm. How long is it?
questions.explanation: 60 mm ÷ 15 mm/s = 4 s. Neonatal records are often reviewed at 15 mm/s; dividing by 30 out of habit gives 2 s and halves every interburst interval.
questions.memoryAid: CHECK THE SPEED first: at 15 mm/s, every mm is TWICE as long in time.
questions.author: NeuroLinea Focus Drills (AI-drafted, fact-checked; requires expert review)

questions.stem: A display is 300 mm wide and set to 30 mm/s. How many seconds does one page show?
questions.explanation: 300 mm ÷ 30 mm/s = 10 s per page, the standard routine EEG page. At 15 mm/s the same width would show 20 s.
questions.memoryAid: 30 mm/s = the 10-second page.
questions.author: NeuroLinea Focus Drills (AI-drafted, fact-checked; requires expert review)

questions.stem: A 10 Hz rhythm is viewed at 30 mm/s, then the timebase is changed to 15 mm/s. What happens?
options: Each wave is 6 mm wide; the rhythm is now 5 Hz
Each wave is 1.5 mm wide; the rhythm is still 10 Hz
Each wave is 3 mm wide; the rhythm is unchanged
Each wave is 1.5 mm wide; the rhythm is now 20 Hz
questions.explanation: At 15 mm/s, a 0.1 s wave takes 15 × 0.1 = 1.5 mm, so the waves are squeezed together and look faster, but the brain is still producing 10 Hz. The timebase changes the picture, never the frequency.
questions.memoryAid: Slower paper = SQUASHED waves that only LOOK faster.
questions.author: NeuroLinea Focus Drills (AI-drafted, fact-checked; requires expert review)

questions.stem: From one peak to the next, a wave takes 0.25 s. What is its frequency?
questions.explanation: Frequency = 1 ÷ period = 1 ÷ 0.25 = 4 Hz. Think: four quarters of a second fit into one second.
questions.memoryAid: Hz = 1 ÷ seconds. A quarter-second wave = FOUR per second.
questions.author: NeuroLinea Focus Drills (AI-drafted, fact-checked; requires expert review)

questions.stem: At 30 mm/s, the R waves in the ECG channel are 25 mm apart. What is the heart rate?
