questions.explanation: 25 ÷ 30 ≈ 0.83 s per beat, and 60 ÷ 0.83 ≈ 72 per minute. Shortcut at 30 mm/s: rate = 1800 ÷ R-R in mm, and 1800 ÷ 25 = 72. 83 reads the 0.83 s as a rate.
questions.memoryAid: Heart rate at 30 mm/s = 1800 ÷ mm between R waves.
questions.author: NeuroLinea Focus Drills (AI-drafted, fact-checked; requires expert review)

questions.stem: A seizure begins at 01:12:40 and ends at 01:13:25. How long did it last?
questions.explanation: From 01:12:40 to 01:13:00 is 20 s, and from 01:13:00 to 01:13:25 is 25 s: 45 s in total. Count up to the whole minute first, then add the rest. 85 s comes from subtracting the times as plain numbers (1325 − 1240), forgetting that a minute has 60 seconds.
questions.memoryAid: Times: COUNT UP to the next whole minute, then add the leftover seconds.
questions.author: NeuroLinea Focus Drills (AI-drafted, fact-checked; requires expert review)

questions.stem: An EEG is sampled at 256 Hz. What is the highest frequency it can represent without aliasing?
questions.explanation: The Nyquist frequency is half the sampling rate: 256 ÷ 2 = 128 Hz. Faster activity aliases, appearing falsely as slower waves.
questions.memoryAid: NYQUIST = HALF. You need at least two samples per wave.
questions.author: NeuroLinea Focus Drills (AI-drafted, fact-checked; requires expert review)

questions.stem: An EEG is sampled at 200 Hz. How much time passes between samples?
questions.explanation: 1000 ms ÷ 200 samples = 5 ms between samples. 200 ms would be one sample every fifth of a second, far too slow for EEG.
questions.memoryAid: Sample interval (ms) = 1000 ÷ sampling rate.
questions.author: NeuroLinea Focus Drills (AI-drafted, fact-checked; requires expert review)

questions.stem: The high-frequency filter is set to 70 Hz. Using the guideline that the sampling rate should be at least three times the HFF, what is the minimum sampling rate?
questions.explanation: 3 × 70 = 210 Hz. Twice the HFF (140) is the bare theoretical Nyquist limit; the extra margin keeps waveforms like spikes from being distorted.
questions.memoryAid: Sampling ≥ 3 × HFF: 70 Hz HFF needs over 200 Hz sampling.
questions.author: NeuroLinea Focus Drills (AI-drafted, fact-checked; requires expert review)

questions.stem: The low-frequency filter is set to 1 Hz. What is the equivalent time constant?
questions.explanation: TC = 1 ÷ (2π × LFF) = 1 ÷ 6.28 ≈ 0.16 s. Shortcut: TC ≈ 0.16 ÷ LFF. 6.3 s multiplies by 2π instead of dividing.
questions.memoryAid: TC ≈ 0.16 ÷ LFF. 1 Hz LFF = 0.16 s, the routine pair.
questions.author: NeuroLinea Focus Drills (AI-drafted, fact-checked; requires expert review)

questions.stem: The low-frequency filter is set to 0.5 Hz. What is the equivalent time constant?
questions.explanation: 0.16 ÷ 0.5 = 0.32 s (often written as 0.3 s). Halving the LFF doubles the time constant, letting more slow activity through.
questions.memoryAid: LOWER LFF = LONGER time constant. Halve one, double the other.
questions.author: NeuroLinea Focus Drills (AI-drafted, fact-checked; requires expert review)

questions.stem: A recording uses a time constant of 0.1 s. What low-frequency filter setting is that?
questions.explanation: LFF ≈ 0.16 ÷ TC = 0.16 ÷ 0.1 = 1.6 Hz. The same 0.16 rule works in both directions.
questions.memoryAid: 0.16 ÷ one = the other (TC and LFF swap places).
questions.author: NeuroLinea Focus Drills (AI-drafted, fact-checked; requires expert review)

questions.stem: The low-frequency filter is raised from 1 Hz to 5 Hz. What happens to 1 Hz delta activity?
options: It is converted into 5 Hz theta
It is unchanged, because the LFF only affects fast activity
It is strongly reduced, so real slowing can be missed
questions.explanation: The LFF (high-pass filter) removes activity below its setting. A 5 Hz LFF strongly attenuates 1 Hz delta, which can hide focal slowing. Filters reduce amplitude; they never change a wave's frequency.
questions.memoryAid: The LOW filter LOSES the LOW frequencies. Raise it and delta fades.
questions.author: NeuroLinea Focus Drills (AI-drafted, fact-checked; requires expert review)

questions.stem: An amplifier has a common mode rejection ratio of 10,000:1. A 20 mV mains signal appears equally at both inputs. How big is it at the output?
questions.explanation: 20 mV = 20,000 µV, and 20,000 ÷ 10,000 = 2 µV. Converting millivolts to microvolts first (× 1000) avoids the decimal-point slips in the other answers.
questions.memoryAid: Convert first: 1 mV = 1000 µV. Then divide by the CMRR.
questions.author: NeuroLinea Focus Drills (AI-drafted, fact-checked; requires expert review)

questions.stem: A CMRR is quoted as 80 dB. What ratio is that?
questions.explanation: For voltage ratios, every 20 dB is a factor of 10: 20 dB = 10, 40 dB = 100, 60 dB = 1,000, 80 dB = 10,000.
questions.memoryAid: Every 20 dB adds a ZERO. 80 dB = four zeros = 10,000.
questions.author: NeuroLinea Focus Drills (AI-drafted, fact-checked; requires expert review)

questions.stem: Input 1 is at −50 µV and input 2 is at −20 µV. What does the channel show?
questions.explanation: Output = input 1 − input 2 = −50 − (−20) = −30 µV. By convention a negative output deflects upward. Adding the two (70) ignores that the amplifier subtracts.
questions.memoryAid: Output = G1 − G2. NEGATIVE goes UP.
questions.author: NeuroLinea Focus Drills (AI-drafted, fact-checked; requires expert review)

questions.stem: During a discharge F3 is at −100 µV and C3 is at −40 µV. What does the F3-C3 channel show?
questions.explanation: F3 − C3 = −100 − (−40) = −60 µV, a 60 µV upward deflection. Subtracting a negative number means adding it back.
questions.memoryAid: Minus a minus is a plus: −100 − (−40) = −60.
questions.author: NeuroLinea Focus Drills (AI-drafted, fact-checked; requires expert review)

questions.stem: A spike gives F7 −40 µV, T3 −80 µV, T5 −40 µV, and 0 µV elsewhere. What do F7-T3 and T3-T5 show?
options: Both flat: the spike is equal in both
Both 40 µV up: no phase reversal
F7-T3 40 µV down and T3-T5 40 µV up: negative phase reversal at T3
F7-T3 40 µV up and T3-T5 40 µV down: positive phase reversal at T3
questions.explanation: F7 − T3 = −40 − (−80) = +40 (down); T3 − T5 = −80 − (−40) = −40 (up). The deflections point toward each other at the shared electrode, T3: a negative phase reversal, which localises the spike's maximum to T3.
questions.memoryAid: Pens POINT AT the negative peak in a bipolar chain.
questions.author: NeuroLinea Focus Drills (AI-drafted, fact-checked; requires expert review)

questions.stem: In a bipolar chain, F3 and C3 are both at −70 µV during a widespread discharge. What does F3-C3 show?
options: 70 µV downward: the second input wins
Flat: the equal potentials cancel out
70 µV upward: each shows its own value
140 µV upward: the two inputs add
questions.explanation: F3 − C3 = −70 − (−70) = 0. A bipolar channel shows only the difference between its two electrodes, so activity equal at both disappears. That is why broad fields can look small in bipolar montages.
questions.memoryAid: Same at both ends = NOTHING in the middle.
questions.author: NeuroLinea Focus Drills (AI-drafted, fact-checked; requires expert review)

questions.stem: In an average reference of 19 electrodes, F4 is at −190 µV during a discharge and every other electrode is at 0 µV. What do the channels show?
options: F4 10 µV up; every other channel 180 µV down
F4 180 µV up; every other channel 10 µV down
F4 190 µV up; every other channel flat
F4 180 µV down; every other channel 10 µV up
questions.explanation: The average is −190 ÷ 19 = −10 µV. F4 − avg = −190 − (−10) = −180 (up). Every other channel is 0 − (−10) = +10 (down): a small false positive deflection everywhere, inherited from the average.
questions.memoryAid: Average reference: every channel = electrode MINUS the mean. A big negative pulls the mean down and paints a fake positive everywhere else.
questions.author: NeuroLinea Focus Drills (AI-drafted, fact-checked; requires expert review)

questions.stem: In an ear reference montage, a left temporal spike also reaches A1 (−40 µV). T3 is at −100 µV and C3 at −20 µV. What do T3-A1 and C3-A1 show?
options: T3-A1 140 µV up; C3-A1 60 µV up
T3-A1 100 µV up; C3-A1 20 µV up
T3-A1 60 µV down; C3-A1 20 µV up
T3-A1 60 µV up; C3-A1 20 µV down
questions.explanation: T3 − A1 = −100 − (−40) = −60 (up, smaller than the true 100). C3 − A1 = −20 − (−40) = +20 (down, the wrong direction). An active reference shrinks nearby spikes and makes quiet channels deflect falsely; check with a bipolar or distant reference.
questions.memoryAid: An ACTIVE ear is a liar: it shrinks the spike next to it and flips the quiet channels.
questions.author: NeuroLinea Focus Drills (AI-drafted, fact-checked; requires expert review)

questions.stem: The nasion-to-inion distance is 35 cm. How far from the nasion is Cz?
questions.explanation: Cz is at 50% of the nasion-inion line: 35 ÷ 2 = 17.5 cm. The line runs Fpz 10%, Fz 30%, Cz 50%, Pz 70%, Oz 90%.
questions.memoryAid: 10, then 20s: Fp 10, F 30, C 50, P 70, O 90 percent.
questions.author: NeuroLinea Focus Drills (AI-drafted, fact-checked; requires expert review)

questions.stem: The nasion-to-inion distance is 35 cm. How far from the nasion is Fz?
questions.explanation: Fz is at 30%: 10% of 35 is 3.5, so 30% is 3 × 3.5 = 10.5 cm. 3.5 cm is Fpz (10%) and 7 cm is 20%, a point with no midline electrode.
questions.memoryAid: Find 10% first (move the decimal), then multiply.
questions.author: NeuroLinea Focus Drills (AI-drafted, fact-checked; requires expert review)

questions.stem: The preauricular-to-preauricular distance is 38 cm. How far from the left preauricular point is C3?
questions.explanation: Along the coronal line: T3 at 10%, C3 at 30%, Cz at 50%. 10% of 38 = 3.8, so 30% = 11.4 cm. 3.8 cm is T3 and 19 cm is Cz.
questions.memoryAid: Ear to ear: T 10, C 30, Cz 50 percent.
questions.author: NeuroLinea Focus Drills (AI-drafted, fact-checked; requires expert review)

questions.stem: The head circumference is 56 cm. What is the distance from Fp1 to F7 along the circumference?
questions.explanation: Around the circumference, Fp1 sits 5% from the midline and then F7, T3, T5 and O1 follow at 10% steps. 10% of 56 = 5.6 cm. 2.8 cm (5%) is the distance from Fpz to Fp1.
questions.memoryAid: Circumference: 5% from the midline to Fp1, then 10% steps.
questions.author: NeuroLinea Focus Drills (AI-drafted, fact-checked; requires expert review)

questions.stem: Epileptiform discharges occur every 0.3 s for 15 s. What frequency is that, and does it meet the ACNS electrographic seizure criterion?
options: About 3.3 Hz for 15 s: it meets the criterion
About 0.3 Hz: periodic discharges, not a seizure
About 3.3 Hz, but too short to count
questions.explanation: 1 ÷ 0.3 ≈ 3.3 Hz. An electrographic seizure is epileptiform discharges averaging more than 2.5 Hz for at least 10 s (or a pattern with definite evolution lasting at least 10 s). 3.3 Hz for 15 s meets it.
questions.memoryAid: Seizure = MORE THAN 2.5 Hz for 10 s or more.
questions.author: NeuroLinea Focus Drills (AI-drafted, fact-checked; requires expert review)

questions.stem: Discharges occur exactly every 0.4 s for 20 s, without evolution. How does this fit the ACNS seizure criterion?
options: 2.5 Hz: not above 2.5 Hz, so not a seizure on frequency alone
0.4 Hz: periodic discharges, far below the seizure range
2.5 Hz: reaching 2.5 Hz is enough, so it is a seizure
4 Hz: well above 2.5 Hz, so it is clearly a seizure
questions.explanation: 1 ÷ 0.4 = 2.5 Hz. The criterion needs MORE than 2.5 Hz, so exactly 2.5 Hz without evolution does not meet it on frequency; periodic discharges between 1 and 2.5 Hz fall in the ictal-interictal continuum.
questions.memoryAid: 2.5 is the line, not the answer: you must be ABOVE it.
questions.author: NeuroLinea Focus Drills (AI-drafted, fact-checked; requires expert review)

questions.stem: Lateralized periodic discharges are present for 21 minutes of a 60-minute epoch. What prevalence term applies?
questions.explanation: 21 ÷ 60 = 35%. ACNS prevalence bands: continuous 90% or more, abundant 50 to 89%, frequent 10 to 49%, occasional 1 to 9%, rare under 1%. 35% is frequent.
questions.memoryAid: Prevalence: Rare <1, Occasional 1-9, Frequent 10-49, Abundant 50-89, Continuous 90+.
questions.author: NeuroLinea Focus Drills (AI-drafted, fact-checked; requires expert review)

questions.stem: Three separate electrographic seizures of 4, 5 and 6 minutes occur within one hour. Is this electrographic status epilepticus?
options: Only if one seizure lasts 30 minutes
Yes: 15 minutes is 25% of the hour
No: it is judged on the longest seizure
No: none of them lasted 10 minutes
questions.explanation: Electrographic status epilepticus is seizure activity for 10 or more continuous minutes, or for a total of 20% or more of any 60-minute period. 4 + 5 + 6 = 15 minutes = 25% of the hour, so it qualifies even though no single seizure lasted 10 minutes.
questions.memoryAid: ESE = 10 straight minutes OR 20% of an hour (12 minutes in total).
questions.author: NeuroLinea Focus Drills (AI-drafted, fact-checked; requires expert review)

questions.stem: A baby was born at 34 weeks' gestation and is now 4 weeks old. What is the postmenstrual age used to interpret the EEG?
questions.explanation: Postmenstrual age = gestational age at birth + age since birth: 34 + 4 = 38 weeks. Neonatal EEG norms are judged by PMA, not by gestational age alone or by weeks since birth.
questions.memoryAid: PMA = born-at + weeks-since. ADD them.
questions.author: NeuroLinea Focus Drills (AI-drafted, fact-checked; requires expert review)
